I *think* the data is more clear post London than pre-London because we no longer end up with artificially high prices (where the price doesn't accurately reflect demand) due to poor gas price oracles. I didn't understand this comment: I was under the impression that 1 would be the minimum. Seems I was wrong given that transactions are included with less. But then why "bug" on the miner? Some miners have configured their minimum inclusion threshold to be lower than what is profitable for them. We should not rely on miners continuing to behave that way. If you want to try to leverage it while the opportunity is present great, but UIs definitely shouldn't rely on it. Ah alright, i was taking bug to have a different meaning Thanks yeah it's more of an "all mining costs considered" approach - not an issue with the implementations. that .01 is probably freeriding for the time being on all the other tx paying 4-7 gwei for priorityFee are there any posts about the potential affects of a deflationary eth and whether it is “good” or “bad”? I'm not sure if it's possible to give an objective "good" or "bad" review. different people with different viewpoints will have differing opinions on the matter I'm not aware of an extensive post, but in general the biggest argument against deflationary currencies is that it leads to hoarding over spending. I think ETH has a few mechanisms to dampen the downsides. First, the gas price market isn't fully ETH-denominated (e.g. 10 gwei at 100$ == 1 gwei at 1000$) Second, ETH is pretty easy to use as collateral for other unit of accounts (e.g. open a loan on maker/aave/etc. and spend DAI vs. ETH) I think the big question is whether it would affect ETH-denominated markets, and the interactions there seem like the hardest to untangle. The first obvious one is staking, which requires 32 ETH. Hopefully we can keep working on lowering that threshold to keep it accessible. The second is anything that usually is priced in ETH, e.g. NFTs. I'm really not sure how increasing the deflationary aspect of ETH affects this, esp. given there is such a "speculation premium" to most of these markets, and whether ETH is deflationary or not may make a negligible difference. Would love to see such an analysis in more detail, though! I have a question about this - I haven't found much else in terms of requirements for a validator node, other than the 32 eth stake. Is there a more detailed article I didn't find? Do you mean what type of machine to run your node on, or why 32 and not another value? hardware - I'm not terribly worried about the staking value I suspect each client would have recommended specs? here's the one for lighthouse: https://lighthouse-book.sigmaprime.io/system-requirements.html it's mostly a point of concern to me from seeing the result on bsc and matic (for example) where it's far from rare that validator nodes can't keep up. I'm reasonably sure that there will be enough validators on eth for a stable infrastructure, though I've wondered about this thank you so much! I suspect other clients would be similar, and worth noting that, post-merge, you'd need to also run an "execution" node (equiv. to a current eth1 node) yeah forgot to mention that - I did see the execution node requirement. about your writeup, on the point of NFTs I personally don't believe deflationary eth to be much of a concern. it would mostly result in price adjustments to happen more often or shift to tokens such as stablecoins. yeah, that's what I think too I'm not sure how many things are "truly" priced in ETH except basically the base fee and the staking requirement judging from the nft circles I'm in it's mostly priced in eth because we strongly believe in ethereum as a whole. we do heavily consider the USD equivalent, however it also depends on the nft. certain communities are fairly unphased by price fluctuations and neither relist on bullish nor bearish markets and neither are the buyers Thinking of deflation, hoarding may not be as much of a problem if you are buying something that is ETH denominated, like an NFT, because you may keep that ETH exposure to enjoy the benefits of the inflation when you expect to sell the NFT. my very rough suspicion for most quality NFT projects is they are priced in "alpha-ETH", meaning that if ETHUSD goes up, they probably appreciate in ETH terms, and if ETHUSD goes down, they probably depreciate in ETH terms. Would be interesting to study the prices of NFTs denominated in ETH as Eth/USD fluctuates Yeah, I think we probably just don't have enough data now because the sample size of NFTs prior to this bull market is tiny _maybe_ the may crash would give some interesting data, but IMO it's very different from, say, a 2 year bear market yeah, interesting to think about I think it heavily depends on the utility connected to the nfts. if it's a pure collector's item or art, I would assume fluctuations to matter more

excerpts.author: butta
excerpts.content: are there any posts about the potential affects of a deflationary eth and whether it is “good” or “bad”?

excerpts.author: not_x912
excerpts.content: I'm not sure if it's possible to give an objective "good" or "bad" review. different people with different viewpoints will have differing opinions on the matter

excerpts.author: timbeiko
excerpts.content: I'm not aware of an extensive post, but in general the biggest argument against deflationary currencies is that it leads to hoarding over spending.

excerpts.author: timbeiko
excerpts.content: I think ETH has a few mechanisms to dampen the downsides.

excerpts.author: timbeiko
excerpts.content: First, the gas price market isn't fully ETH-denominated (e.g. 10 gwei at 100$ == 1 gwei at 1000$)

excerpts.author: timbeiko
excerpts.content: Second, ETH is pretty easy to use as collateral for other unit of accounts (e.g. open a loan on maker/aave/etc. and spend DAI vs. ETH)

excerpts.author: timbeiko
excerpts.content: I think the big question is whether it would affect ETH-denominated markets, and the interactions there seem like the hardest to untangle.

excerpts.author: timbeiko
excerpts.content: The first obvious one is staking, which requires 32 ETH. Hopefully we can keep working on lowering that threshold to keep it accessible.

excerpts.author: timbeiko
excerpts.content: The second is anything that usually is priced in ETH, e.g. NFTs. I'm really not sure  how increasing the deflationary aspect of ETH affects this, esp. given there is such a "speculation premium" to most of these markets, and whether ETH is deflationary or not may make a negligible difference.

excerpts.author: timbeiko
excerpts.content: Would love to see such an analysis in more detail, though!

excerpts.author: not_x912
excerpts.content: I have a question about this - I haven't found much else in terms of requirements for a validator node, other than the 32 eth stake. Is there a more detailed article I didn't find?

excerpts.content: Do you mean what type of machine to run your node on, or why 32 and not another value?

excerpts.content: hardware - I'm not terribly worried about the staking value

excerpts.author: timbeiko
excerpts.content: I suspect each client would have recommended specs?

excerpts.author: timbeiko
excerpts.content: here's the one for lighthouse: https://lighthouse-book.sigmaprime.io/system-requirements.html

excerpts.author: not_x912
excerpts.content: it's mostly a point of concern to me from seeing the result on bsc and matic (for example) where it's far from rare that validator nodes can't keep up. I'm reasonably sure that there will be enough validators on eth for a stable infrastructure, though I've wondered about this

excerpts.author: not_x912
excerpts.content: thank you so much!

excerpts.content: I suspect other clients would be similar, and worth noting that, post-merge, you'd need to also run an "execution" node (equiv. to a current eth1 node)

excerpts.author: not_x912
excerpts.content: yeah forgot to mention that - I did see the execution node requirement.

excerpts.author: not_x912
excerpts.content: about your writeup, on the point of NFTs I personally don't believe deflationary eth to be much of a concern. it would mostly result in price adjustments to happen more often or shift to tokens such as stablecoins.

excerpts.author: timbeiko
excerpts.content: yeah, that's what I think too

excerpts.author: timbeiko
excerpts.content: I'm not sure how many things are "truly" priced in ETH

excerpts.author: timbeiko
excerpts.content: except basically the base fee and the staking requirement

excerpts.author: not_x912
excerpts.content: judging from the nft circles I'm in it's mostly priced in eth because we strongly believe in ethereum as a whole. we do heavily consider the USD equivalent, however

excerpts.author: not_x912
excerpts.content: it also depends on the nft. certain communities are fairly unphased by price fluctuations and neither relist on bullish nor bearish markets and neither are the buyers

excerpts.content: Thinking of deflation, hoarding may not be as much of a problem if you are buying something that is ETH denominated, like an NFT, because you may keep that ETH exposure to enjoy the benefits of the inflation when you expect to sell the NFT.

excerpts.content: Would be interesting to study the prices of NFTs denominated in ETH as Eth/USD fluctuates
